title: Natural Hazards and Disaster Preparedness

standard_text: Natural hazards, disasters, prevention and mitigation, preparedness and adaptation: hazard, exposure, vulnerability and risk; hazard maps and early warning systems; disaster risk reduction and management; climate change adaptation. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, General Science, Term 3)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 General Science worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Term 3): hazards and risk, hazard maps and early warnings, mitigation, preparedness and adaptation. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Risk depends on hazard, exposure and vulnerability.
body_html:
How to think about it

A hazard is an event that may cause harm (earthquake, typhoon, flood, eruption); a disaster happens when a hazard seriously disrupts a community. Risk depends on the hazard, how exposed people are, and how vulnerable they are; it is reduced by building capacity.

Mitigation reduces impacts before they happen (building codes, dikes, mangrove planting). Preparedness means plans, drills, go bags and following PAGASA and PHIVOLCS warnings. Adaptation adjusts how we live to a changing climate. The NDRRMC and local DRRM offices coordinate disaster risk reduction.

Example

Planting mangroves along a coast is an example of?

Before the disaster

Answer: mitigation

Example

A family packs a go bag. Is it mitigation or preparedness?

Plans and supplies

Answer: preparedness

Common mistakes

  • Thinking hazards and disasters are the same.
  • Thinking disasters cannot be reduced.
  • Waiting until a disaster to make a plan.

items.q: Rafael's data shows that a river gauge shows water rising after days of heavy rain upstream. Which hazard is most likely to follow?
items.e: Monitoring warning signs helps scientists forecast hazards.

items.q: Joy's data shows that months without rain and very dry, windy weather. Which hazard is most likely to follow?
items.e: Monitoring warning signs helps scientists forecast hazards.

items.q: What is climate change adaptation?
c: adjusting how we live to reduce harm from a changing climate
items.e: Examples: drought-tolerant crops and raised houses in flood areas.

items.q: Christian's town wants to reduce damage from floods. Which technology would help most?
c: levees, floodplain maps and raised buildings
Doppler radar warnings and underground shelters
gas and tilt sensors with evacuation plans
retaining walls, drainage and planting trees on slopes
items.e: Mitigation technology matches the hazard.

items.q: What is a disaster?
c: a small earthquake no one felt
a serious disruption of a community causing losses it cannot cope with on its own
items.e: Disasters happen when hazards meet vulnerable communities.

items.q: Which usually takes longer: a glacier carving a valley or a mountain range rising?
c: They take exactly the same time.
items.e: Plate-scale changes are the slowest.

items.q: Isabel's town wants to reduce damage from wildfires. Which technology would help most?
c: cleared defensible space around homes and fire-resistant roofs
buildings with base isolators and flexible steel frames
storm shutters, stronger roof straps and early warnings from satellites
gas and tilt sensors with evacuation plans
items.e: Mitigation technology matches the hazard.

items.q: What is disaster preparedness?
c: planning and practicing what to do before a disaster
items.e: Examples: go bags, drills and evacuation plans.

items.q: Risk depends on which factors?
c: hazard, exposure and vulnerability (reduced by capacity)
items.e: Reducing exposure and vulnerability lowers risk.

items.q: Bianca's town wants to reduce damage from tsunamis. Which technology would help most?
c: storm shutters, stronger roof straps and early warnings from satellites
Doppler radar warnings and underground shelters
levees, floodplain maps and raised buildings
ocean buoys and warning sirens with marked evacuation routes
items.e: Mitigation technology matches the hazard.

items.q: Which usually happens faster: a glacier carving a valley or a sand dune moving across a desert?
c: They take exactly the same time.
a sand dune moving across a desert
items.e: Earth processes range from seconds to hundreds of millions of years.

items.q: Nico's town wants to reduce damage from volcanic eruptions. Which technology would help most?
c: retaining walls, drainage and planting trees on slopes
gas and tilt sensors with evacuation plans
storm shutters, stronger roof straps and early warnings from satellites
buildings with base isolators and flexible steel frames
items.e: Mitigation technology matches the hazard.

items.q: Which usually happens faster: a river delta growing or a volcanic eruption building a new cone?
c: They take exactly the same time.
a volcanic eruption building a new cone
items.e: Earth processes range from seconds to hundreds of millions of years.

items.q: What does vulnerability mean?
c: how easily people or things can be harmed by a hazard
items.e: Poor housing and living near rivers increase vulnerability.

items.q: Which usually happens faster: a glacier carving a valley or a mountain range rising?
c: They take exactly the same time.
items.e: Earth processes range from seconds to hundreds of millions of years.

items.q: What is a hazard?
c: a dangerous event or condition that may cause loss of life or damage
a disaster that has already happened
items.e: A hazard becomes a disaster when it seriously harms a community.

items.q: Diane's data shows that heavy rain soaks a steep hillside that lost its trees in a fire. Which hazard is most likely to follow?
items.e: Monitoring warning signs helps scientists forecast hazards.

items.q: What is the difference between hazard and risk?
c: a hazard is a possible source of harm; risk combines how likely it is and how severe the consequences are
a hazard is always a disaster
risk is the cause and hazard is the result
items.e: Risk = likelihood × consequence.

items.q: Kenneth's data shows that the sea quickly pulls back far from the beach after strong shaking. Which hazard is most likely to follow?
items.e: Monitoring warning signs helps scientists forecast hazards.

items.q: What is disaster mitigation?
c: actions that reduce the impact of hazards before they happen
items.e: Examples: building codes, dikes and planting mangroves.

What should a family go bag contain?
c: water, food, flashlight, radio, first aid kit, medicines and copies of documents
items.e: It should last for at least three days.

items.e: Each step of 1 is ×10 in amplitude: 10^(7 − 4.5) = 316 times.

What are hazard maps used for?
c: to show areas at risk of floods, landslides, storm surges and other hazards
items.e: The NOAH and HazardHunterPH tools show Philippine hazard maps.

items.e: 80 × 8 = 640 km. Three stations are needed to locate the epicenter.

What is an early warning system?
c: a way of detecting hazards and warning people so that they can act in time
items.e: PAGASA signals and PHIVOLCS alerts are early warnings.

items.q: Why is building on steep, deforested slopes risky?
c: landslides are more likely after heavy rain
items.e: Tree roots hold soil in place.

items.q: Why are mangroves important for coastal hazard reduction?
c: their roots reduce wave energy and storm surge
items.e: Mangroves are a natural barrier.

items.q: At a seismic station the S-waves arrive 40 s after the P-waves. Using 8 km of distance for each second of lag, how far away is the epicenter?
items.e: 40 × 8 = 320 km. Three stations are needed to locate the epicenter.

items.q: About how many times more energy is released by a magnitude 10 earthquake than a magnitude 7 earthquake? (Each step of 1 is about 32 times the energy.)
How many times larger is the ground motion (wave amplitude) of a magnitude 6.5 earthquake than a magnitude 3 earthquake?
items.e: Each step of 1 is ×10 in amplitude: 10^(6.5 − 3) = 3.16e+03 times.

items.q: Corals turn white and die in hot summers. Which climate change is this evidence of?
items.e: Many independent kinds of evidence point the same way.

items.q: A community plans monitoring gas and ground swelling to warn people. Which hazard is this mainly meant to reduce?
items.e: Match the plan to the hazard.

items.q: After a flood, why should you avoid wading in floodwater?
c: it may carry disease such as leptospirosis and hidden dangers
items.e: Leptospirosis spreads through rat urine in floodwater.

items.q: What is the purpose of an evacuation center?
c: a safe place for people to stay during and after a disaster
items.e: Schools and covered courts are often used.

items.q: Kenneth's family makes a storm kit. Which should go in it?
items.e: A storm kit has things you need if the power goes out.

items.q: There is a flood. Which is NOT safe?
c: leave if told to, or stay inside away from windows
move to higher ground and stay out of the water
drink water and stay in the shade or inside
items.e: Drive through deep water is not safe in a flood.

items.e: Geologic hazards come from processes inside the Earth.

items.q: Which action best reduces the risk to people from wildfires?
c: water conservation and storing water in reservoirs
clearing brush to make defensible space around homes
building codes that make structures flexible and strong
zoning that keeps homes off the floodplain
items.e: Hazards cannot be stopped, but their harm can be reduced.

items.q: After a flood, Vincent sees puddles in the street. What should he do?
items.e: Stay safe after a storm too.

items.q: What does 'resilience' mean in disaster management?
c: the ability of a community to resist, cope with and recover from a disaster
items.e: Resilient communities bounce back faster.

items.q: After a heat wave day, Kyla feels very hot and tired. What should she do?
c: rest in a cool place and drink water
items.e: Stay safe after a storm too.

items.q: After a storm, Patricia sees a fallen power line. What should she do?

items.e: Stay safe after a storm too.

items.q: There is a hurricane. Which is NOT safe?

leave if told to, or stay inside away from windows
items.e: Go surfing is not safe in a hurricane.

items.q: There is a hurricane. Which is NOT safe?

items.q: Which is an example of a hydrometeorological hazard?
items.e: Hydrometeorological hazards come from weather and water.

items.q: Coastal towns flood more often at high tide. Which climate change is this evidence of?

items.q: Angelo's family makes a storm kit. Which does NOT belong?

items.q: There is a flood. What should Sheila do?

items.q: What is a pyroclastic flow?
c: a fast-moving, very hot flow of gas, ash and rock from an eruption
